chapter_note.about: k-nearest neighbours predicts a new point by looking at the training points closest to it. To classify, the k nearest points vote. To predict a number, you average their targets. There is no training step, and the behaviour is controlled by the distance you use and by k. This chapter covers distances, voting, the effect of k, regression, leave-one-out error, scaling, high dimensions, the cost of prediction and the nearest-centroid shortcut.

chapter_note.simple: k-nearest neighbours is the 'ask your neighbours' method. To label a new point, you find the k training points closest to it and let them vote. If you are predicting a number, you average their numbers instead. There is no learning step. The method keeps the data and does all the work when a question arrives. Small k follows every wiggle and large k smooths everything out. The features must be on the same scale and not too many, or 'closest' stops meaning anything.

cards.title: Distance
cards.simple: Distance tells k-NN who counts as 'near'. Think of walking to a friend's house. If you could fly in a straight line, the distance is the straight line (Euclidean). If you must follow the city blocks, it is the number of blocks you walk along the streets (Manhattan). To find the nearest friend you only need the order of the distances. Squaring every distance keeps the same order and saves you from taking square roots. In exam words: Euclidean = √(sum of squared gaps), Manhattan = sum of absolute gaps, and you can rank by squared distance.
cards.idea: k-NN needs a way to say how far apart two points are. The usual choice is **Euclidean distance**, the length of the straight line between them. **Manhattan distance** adds up the horizontal and vertical steps instead. To find the nearest point you only need the order of the distances, so you can compare **squared** Euclidean distances and skip the square root.
cards.definition:
$$d_2(p,q)=\sqrt{\sum_i (p_i-q_i)^2},\qquad d_1(p,q)=\sum_i |p_i-q_i|$$

Symbols: $p$ and $q$ are two points, and $p_i$, $q_i$ are their $i$-th coordinates (features). $d_2$ is Euclidean distance and $d_1$ is Manhattan distance. Ranking by $d_2^2=\sum_i(p_i-q_i)^2$ gives the same order as ranking by $d_2$.
cards.intuition_full: Euclidean distance is Pythagoras extended to any number of coordinates: square each gap, add, take the square root. In two dimensions it is the hypotenuse. Manhattan distance is the length of the two legs added together, which is the walk along city blocks. The square root never changes which point is nearest, because a bigger number always has a bigger square root. So in exam questions you can compare the sums of squares and take the root only if the question asks for the actual distance. The two distances can disagree about who is nearest. A point on the diagonal is closer in a straight line than the same point measured along the blocks. Unless the question names another distance, use Euclidean.

example.setup: The query is q = (0, 0). Point P is (3, 3) and point Q is (5, 0). Which is nearer to q by Euclidean distance, and which by Manhattan distance?
steps: Euclidean, squared. P: 3² + 3² = 9 + 9 = 18. Q: 5² + 0² = 25.
18 < 25, so P is nearer by Euclidean distance. (Actual distances: √18 ≈ 4.24 and 5.)
5 < 6, so Q is nearer by Manhattan distance.
The two distances disagree. The metric you use decides the neighbour.
example.answer: Euclidean picks P (18 < 25). Manhattan picks Q (5 < 6).

(c) Manhattan. P1: 3 + 0 + 0 = 3. P2: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. P3: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5. The smallest is 3, so P1.

examples.setup: A point is at (3, −3) and the query is at (0, 0). Find the Manhattan distance and the Euclidean distance. A student adds the signed gaps and gets 0. What went wrong?
steps: Manhattan uses the absolute value of each gap: |3| + |−3| = 3 + 3 = 6.
The student added 3 + (−3) = 0. Opposite signs cancel, which would say the point sits on the query. That is absurd.
Euclidean squares each gap, so signs vanish: 3² + (−3)² = 9 + 9 = 18, and √18 ≈ 4.24.
examples.answer: Manhattan distance 6 and Euclidean distance √18 ≈ 4.24. Always take absolute values or squares before adding.

cards.title: Majority vote
cards.simple: Imagine you are new in town and want a restaurant. You ask the 3 people who live nearest to you. Two say 'the pizza place' and one says 'the burger place', so you go for pizza. If you had asked 5 people the answer might change. With only two choices, ask an odd number of neighbours so the vote can never tie. And always count the votes yourself instead of trusting the very first person. In exam words: k-NN predicts the most common label among the k nearest points, and the answer can change as k changes.
cards.idea: To classify a query, **sort the training points by distance**, take the k nearest, and let them **vote**. The label with the most votes wins. For two classes an odd k avoids ties. The answer can change as k grows, so check every k the question asks about.
cards.definition:
$$\hat y(q)=\arg\max_{c}\ \bigl|\{\,i\in N_k(q):\ y_i=c\,\}\bigr|$$

Symbols: $N_k(q)$ is the set of the $k$ training points nearest to the query $q$. $y_i$ is the label of training point $i$. The argmax picks the class $c$ with the most points in that neighbourhood.
cards.intuition_full: A single nearest neighbour is easy to mislead: one odd point close to the query decides everything. Taking k neighbours lets the local majority speak. The vote counts how many of the k nearest belong to each class, and the biggest count wins. Because points are added in order of distance, the vote at k = 3 includes the vote at k = 1, and the vote at k = 5 includes k = 3. A close pair of points of one class can win at small k, and a bigger group of the other class can win once k is large enough to reach it. That is why GATE questions ask for the minimum odd k that flips the answer. You list the points by distance and vote at k = 1, 3, 5 and so on. The distances only need to be ranked, so squared distances will do.

example.setup: The query is at (0, 0). Training points: (1, 1) A, (0, 2) A, (−2, 1) B, (3, 0) B, (0, −3) B and (4, 4) A. Find the prediction for k = 1, 3 and 5, and the smallest odd k at which the label becomes B.
steps: Sorted by distance: A (2), A (4), B (5), B (9), B (9), A (32).
k = 1: the nearest is A. Votes A 1, B 0. Predict A.
k = 3: A, A, B. Votes A 2, B 1. Predict A.
k = 5: A, A, B, B, B. Votes A 2, B 3. Predict B. The smallest odd k for B is 5.
example.answer: k = 1 gives A, k = 3 gives A, k = 5 gives B. The minimum odd k for B is 5.

k = 5: A, A, B, A, B gives A 3, B 2: A.
k = 7: all seven points. A 3, B 4: B.

cards.title: Effect of k
cards.simple: Think about asking neighbours for advice again. If you ask only your single nearest neighbour, you get a very personal answer. It follows one person's taste, even if that person is odd, and it changes completely if one person moves house. If you ask the whole town, you get 'whatever most people like', the same answer for everyone, which is calm but ignores local differences. The best choice sits in between. In exam words: small k gives low bias and high variance; large k gives high bias and low variance; k = n predicts the majority class everywhere.
cards.idea: k controls how local the vote is. **Small k** follows every nearby point, including noisy ones: a jagged boundary, low bias, high variance, and overfitting. **Large k** averages over many points: a smooth boundary, high bias, low variance, and underfitting. With **k = n** every query gets the majority class of the whole training set. Choose k by cross-validation.
cards.definition:
$$k=1:\ \text{most flexible}\qquad\qquad k=n:\ \text{one constant answer}$$

Symbols: $k$ is the number of neighbours that vote and $n$ is the number of training points. The model gets simpler as $k$ grows, so the complexity of k-NN goes like $1/k$. At $k=1$ the training error is 0. At $k=n$ the prediction is the majority class.
cards.intuition_full: In the bias and variance chapter, flexibility lowers bias and raises variance. For k-NN the flexibility dial is k, and it turns the opposite way: smaller k means more flexible. With k = 1 the prediction at any spot is the label of the single nearest point, so one mislabelled point carves out a little island of the wrong class. That is variance: change the sample slightly and the boundary changes. With k = 3 that lone point is outvoted by its two neighbours, so the island disappears. With k = n the vote ignores the query altogether and every query gets the majority label. That is bias: the model cannot see local structure. The test error is U-shaped between the two extremes, so an intermediate k is best.

example.setup: Nine training points on a line at x = 0 to 8 have labels A, A, A, B, A, A, B, B, B (the B at x = 3 is noise). Predict the label at each of these nine positions with k = 1, 3 and 9. Count how many predictions differ from the data.
steps: The data: A A A B A A B B B. The lone B at x = 3 sits among A's.
k = 1: each point's nearest neighbour is itself, so the predictions copy the data. 0 differ. The noisy B is faithfully reproduced.
k = 3 at x = 3: the three nearest are x = 2 (A), x = 3 (B), x = 4 (A). Votes A 2, B 1: A. The noise is outvoted. The other positions are unchanged, so the row is A A A A A A B B B. 1 differs.
k = 9: all nine points vote. A 5, B 4: A everywhere. The four B's are overruled. 4 differ.
Small k copies the noise. Large k smooths away real structure. k = 3 sits in between.
example.answer: k = 1: 0 differ, k = 3: 1 differs, k = 9: 4 differ. Small k is jagged, k = n is a constant.

cards.title: k-NN regression
cards.simple: Suppose you want to guess the price of a flat. You look at the 3 flats closest to yours in size and take the average of their prices. That is k-NN regression. Instead of voting, you average the numbers. One thing to remember: closeness is judged using the inputs (size), and the average is taken over the outputs (price). Mixing these up is the classic slip. In exam words: k-NN regression predicts the mean of the targets of the k nearest neighbours.
cards.idea: For regression, k-NN predicts the **average of the targets** of the k nearest neighbours. Distances are measured on the inputs x. The averaging is done on the outputs y. A small k follows the data closely. A large k gives a smoother, flatter prediction.
cards.definition:
$$\hat y(q)=\frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(q)}y_i$$

Symbols: $N_k(q)$ is the set of the $k$ training points whose inputs $x$ are nearest to the query $q$. $y_i$ is the target (output) of training point $i$.
cards.intuition_full: Classification asks 'which label is most common nearby?' Regression asks 'what is the typical value nearby?' The typical value is the mean. The input x only decides who the neighbours are. Once you have them, you ignore x and average their y values. With k = n every query gets the mean of all targets, a flat line. This is the same smoothing story as before: small k means low bias and high variance, large k means high bias and low variance. A far-away outlier target only affects queries that have it as a neighbour.

cards.title: Training and leave-one-out error
cards.simple: A student who memorises the answer key scores 100% on a practice sheet. That does not mean they know the subject. k-NN with k = 1 is that student. If you test it on its own training points, each point is its own nearest neighbour and always gets the right label. A perfect score that proves nothing. For an honest score, hide each point in turn and predict it from the others. That is leave-one-out. In exam words: 1-NN training error is 0; use leave-one-out, excluding the point itself, to estimate the real error.
cards.idea: Test a k-NN classifier on its own training points with k = 1 and each point finds **itself** at distance 0. The training error is **0**, which says nothing about new data. For an honest estimate use **leave-one-out**: hide each point, find its nearest neighbours among the **others**, and count the mistakes.
cards.definition:
$$\text{LOO error}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\!\left[\hat y_{-i}(x_i)\neq y_i\right]$$

Symbols: $\hat y_{-i}(x_i)$ is the prediction for sample $i$ using all samples except $i$. The bracket $\mathbf 1[\cdot]$ is 1 for a mistake and 0 for a correct prediction. k-NN needs no refitting, so LOO is cheap: just recompute the neighbours without the held-out point.
cards.intuition_full: Training error rewards memory. For 1-NN, memory is perfect: the nearest point to a training point is itself. So the training error is exactly 0 unless two identical points carry different labels. For k > 1 the point still counts as one of its own k neighbours, which flatters the score. Leave-one-out removes the flattery. Each point is predicted as if it were new. Because k-NN stores the data and does no fitting, 'refitting n times' costs nothing extra: only the neighbour lists change. This is why leave-one-out is the natural way to choose k for k-NN. When doing it by hand, be strict about the rule: the held-out point must not be in the pool.

example.setup: Six points on a line at x = 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8 have labels A, A, A, B, B, A. For 1-NN, find the training error and the leave-one-out error.
steps: Training error: every point's nearest neighbour is itself, at distance 0. All six predictions are right. Training error = 0 / 6 = 0.
LOO, x = 0, 1, 2 (all A): the nearest other points are x = 1, x = 0 or 2, and x = 1. All A. Right, right, right.
LOO, x = 5 and 6 (B): each is the other's nearest neighbour, at distance 1. Both B. Right, right.
LOO, x = 8 (A): the nearest other point is x = 6 (B, distance 2). Predict B. Wrong.
LOO error = 1 wrong out of 6 = 1/6 ≈ 0.167.

cards.title: Feature scaling
cards.simple: Suppose you rank people by 'closeness' using age in years and income in rupees. A one-year age gap counts as 1. A ₹1,000 income gap counts as 1,000. When you add the gaps up, income completely swamps age, as if age did not exist. To be fair, put both on the same scale first, for example by measuring each as 'how many typical steps above or below the average'. Then each feature gets a fair say. In exam words: k-NN needs scaled features, otherwise the feature with the largest numeric range dominates the distance.
cards.idea: Distance adds up squared gaps, so a feature measured in big numbers (income in rupees) drowns a feature measured in small numbers (age in years). The neighbours are then chosen by income alone. **Scale the features first**: standardise (subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation) or rescale to the range 0 to 1. Then each feature gets a fair say.
cards.definition:
$$z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x'=\frac{x-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}$$

Symbols: $\mu$ is the mean of the feature, $\sigma$ its standard deviation, and $x_{\min}$, $x_{\max}$ its smallest and largest values. Work out these numbers on the training data, then apply them to the training points and to the query.
cards.intuition_full: Euclidean distance treats a gap of 1 in any feature as equal to a gap of 1 in any other. That is only fair if the features are measured on comparable scales. A feature with a range of 100,000 produces squared gaps that can be a billion times bigger than a feature with a range of 40. The small feature then contributes nothing, and k-NN is effectively using one feature. Standardising turns each feature into 'standard deviations from the mean', so a gap of 1 means one typical step for every feature. Min-max scaling squeezes each feature into 0 to 1. Either works. The statistics are learned from the training data and reused for the query, never recomputed from the query alone.

example.setup: A query q has age 25 and income ₹40,000. Person A is age 55 with income ₹40,500. Person B is age 26 with income ₹46,000. Which is nearer to q using raw Euclidean distance? Then standardise (age: mean 40, sd 10; income: mean ₹50,000, sd ₹20,000) and check again.
steps: Raw gaps. A: age 30, income 500. B: age 1, income 6,000.
Raw distances. A: √(30² + 500²) = √(900 + 250,000) ≈ 500.9. B: √(1² + 6,000²) ≈ 6,000. So A looks nearer, although A is 30 years older.
Why: the income gap squared (250,000 for A, 36,000,000 for B) is huge. The age gap (900 or 1) barely counts.
Scaled distances. A: √(3.0² + 0.025²) ≈ 3.00. B: √(0.1² + 0.3²) = √0.10 ≈ 0.32. Now B is nearer.
example.answer: Raw: A is nearer (500.9 < 6,000). After scaling: B is nearer (0.32 < 3.00). Scaling changed the neighbour.

cards.title: High dimensions
cards.simple: In a long corridor, finding the nearest person is easy: some people are close and some are far. Now imagine a giant hall with a thousand directions, and every person is standing roughly the same far distance from you. There is no real 'nearest' person, so picking one is almost random. K-NN has the same trouble when there are many features, especially useless ones: the nearest point is hardly nearer than the farthest. In exam words: in high dimensions distances concentrate, so 'nearest' loses meaning, and irrelevant features make it worse.
cards.idea: With **many features**, the distances from a query to all training points become nearly equal. The nearest neighbour is hardly nearer than the farthest, so neighbours stop being informative. **Irrelevant features** add noise to every distance. Fixes: choose or compress the features (feature selection, PCA), collect more data, or scale the relevant features.
cards.definition:
$$\text{contrast}=\frac{d_{\text{far}}}{d_{\text{near}}}\ \longrightarrow\ 1\quad\text{as irrelevant features are added}$$

Symbols: $d_{\text{near}}$ and $d_{\text{far}}$ are the distances from the query to a near and a far training point. If every irrelevant feature adds roughly the same amount $c$ to every squared distance, then after $m$ such features $d^2_{\text{near}}\to d^2_{\text{near}}+mc$ and $d^2_{\text{far}}\to d^2_{\text{far}}+mc$.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the squared distance as a sum of contributions, one per feature. A useful feature contributes a lot for points that really differ and little for points that are alike. An irrelevant feature contributes about the same random amount to every point, near or far. When you add m of those equal amounts to both squared distances, the shared part grows with m and swamps the difference. The ratio of far to near squared distance (9 + mc) / (1 + mc) moves toward 1. Concretely, a point 3 times farther than another becomes only 4% farther after enough noise features. With many dimensions even relevant features can behave like this for random data, which is why k-NN needs far more samples as d grows. The cure is fewer, better features.

example.setup: On the one useful feature, the query has a near point A at distance 1 and a far point B at distance 3. Suppose every irrelevant feature adds 4 to the squared distance of both points. Find the far ÷ near distance ratio with m = 0, 1, 4 and 24 irrelevant features.
steps: m = 0: squared distances are 1 and 9. Distances 1.0 and 3.0. Ratio 3.0.
m = 1: squared distances 1 + 4 = 5 and 9 + 4 = 13. Distances 2.2 and 3.6. Ratio 3.6 / 2.2 = 1.61.
m = 4: 1 + 16 = 17 and 9 + 16 = 25. Distances 4.1 and 5.0. Ratio 1.21.
B started 3 times farther and ends only 4% farther. 'Nearest' now carries almost no information.
example.answer: The ratio falls from 3.0 to 1.04. Irrelevant features wash out the difference between near and far.

cards.title: Lazy learning and cost
cards.simple: Some students prepare a summary before the exam. That is training. A k-NN student prepares nothing. They just keep all the books. When a question arrives, they flip through every book page to find the examples that look most similar. So there is no homework before the exam, but every answer takes a long time, and the more books there are, the longer it takes. In exam words: k-NN is a lazy learner. It has no training phase, and each prediction costs about n × d operations.
cards.idea: k-NN does **no real training**. It simply stores the data. All the work happens when a query arrives: compute the distance to all n stored points (each over d features), then pick the k smallest. That costs about $n\times d$ operations **per query**, and the memory to keep every training point. It is cheap to build and expensive to use.
cards.definition:
$$\text{training}=\text{store the data},\qquad \text{prediction}=O(n\,d)\ \text{per query},\qquad \text{memory}=O(n\,d)$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of training points and $d$ the number of features. Picking the $k$ smallest of $n$ distances adds a little more (sorting costs $O(n\log n)$), but $n\,d$ is the dominant term. Adding a new training point needs no retraining.
cards.intuition_full: Most models learn a summary (weights, a tree, a line) from the data, and then throw the data away. Predicting is fast because the summary is small. k-NN skips the summary and keeps the data itself as its model. That is why it is called lazy or instance-based: the work is put off until a query arrives. The cost per query is the number of distance computations, n, times the cost of each, d coordinate differences. Doubling n doubles the work. Doubling d also doubles it. There is a bright side: updating the model is free, because adding a point is just appending a row. The dark side is that prediction time and memory grow with the data, so very large datasets need indexing tricks that work best in few dimensions.

example.setup: Five training points (x1, x2): P1 (1,1), P2 (4,3), P3 (2,7), P4 (5,5), P5 (3,2). A query arrives at q = (2, 3). Do the work of 3-NN, and count the cost.
steps: Training: nothing to do. The table of five points is just stored.
At prediction time, compute 5 squared distances to q. P1: 1 + 4 = 5. P2: 4 + 0 = 4. P3: 0 + 16 = 16. P4: 9 + 4 = 13. P5: 1 + 1 = 2.
The k = 3 smallest are 2, 4 and 5: P5, P2 and P1.
Cost per query: n × d = 5 × 2 = 10 coordinate differences.
Scale up: n = 10,000 and d = 20 gives 10,000 × 20 = 200,000 per query. For 500 queries that is 500 × 200,000 = 100,000,000 = 10⁸.
example.answer: No training. About n × d = 10 operations per query here, and 200,000 per query at n = 10,000, d = 20.

cards.title: Nearest centroid
cards.simple: Instead of remembering every student, the school keeps just the average position of each class, a single centre point for class A and one for class B. A new student joins the class whose centre is nearer. The dividing line between the two classes is the line of points exactly halfway between the two centres, a perpendicular line through the middle. Even though distances involve squares, the squared parts cancel out in the comparison, so that dividing line is perfectly straight. In exam words: nearest-centroid classifier; f(x) = ‖x − μ1‖² − ‖x − μ2‖² is linear in x.
cards.idea: A **nearest-centroid** classifier replaces the whole training set by one average point (a **centroid**) per class. A query goes to the class whose centroid is nearest. The boundary is the set of points equally far from both centroids: the **perpendicular bisector** of the segment joining them. It is a straight line (a flat plane in more dimensions), because the squared terms cancel.
cards.definition:
$$f(x)=\|x-\mu_1\|^2-\|x-\mu_2\|^2=\|\mu_1\|^2-\|\mu_2\|^2+2\,x^{\top}(\mu_2-\mu_1)$$

Symbols: $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are the class centroids (the mean of each class's points). $\|\cdot\|^2$ is squared length. Predict class 1 if $f(x)<0$ (nearer to $\mu_1$) and class 2 if $f(x)>0$. The $\|x\|^2$ terms cancel, so $f$ is linear in $x$.
cards.intuition_full: Expand each squared distance: ‖x − μ‖² = ‖x‖² − 2x·μ + ‖μ‖². In the difference f(x), the term ‖x‖² appears in both and cancels. What is left is a constant plus a dot product with the vector from μ1 to μ2. A function that is a constant plus a dot product is linear, so the set where it equals zero is a straight line in two dimensions, or a flat plane in more. It passes through the midpoint of the two centroids and is at right angles to the segment joining them. This classifier is the simplest summary of each class. It ignores how spread out a class is, which is its weakness. With equal priors and the same identity covariance for both classes it matches the LDA rule.

example.setup: Class 1 has points (1, 1) and (3, 1). Class 2 has points (5, 3) and (7, 5). Find the centroids, classify the query x = (3, 3), and find the boundary.
steps: 5 < 10, so x goes to class 1. Here f(x) = 5 − 10 = −5 < 0.
Boundary: halfway point (4, 2.5), perpendicular to the segment from (2,1) to (6,4). In formula form f(x) = 5 − 52 + 2x·(4, 3) = 8x1 + 6x2 − 47.
Check: f(3, 3) = 24 + 18 − 47 = −5, the same as before. The boundary 8x1 + 6x2 = 47 passes through (4, 2.5), since 32 + 15 = 47.
example.answer: Centroids (2, 1) and (6, 4). The query is class 1. The boundary is the line 8x1 + 6x2 = 47.

The two classifiers disagree. The centroid of class 1, (5, 0), is far from any class 1 point, because that class is spread out.
examples.answer: 1-NN says class 1. Nearest centroid says class 2. A spread-out class is poorly described by its mean.

Compute the squared distance from the query to each centroid.
Assign the class with the smaller distance, or use the sign of f(x).
The boundary is the perpendicular bisector: a straight line.
cards.mistake: Calling the nearest-centroid boundary quadratic. The squares ‖x‖² cancel in f(x), leaving a linear function.

With more than two classes, boundaries are pieces of perpendicular bisectors.
The classifier ignores how spread out or unequal the classes are.
With equal priors and identity covariance it matches the LDA rule.

k-means clustering: centroids are the same class means.

Foundations: Algebra. Expanding squares and cancelling equal terms.

scenes.title: Euclidean and Manhattan can pick different neighbours

objects.text: Euclid picks P.   Manhattan picks Q.

steps.caption: The query q is at the origin. P is at (3, 3) and Q is at (5, 0). Which one is nearer? It depends on how we measure.
Euclidean: the straight line. Squared distance to P is 3² + 3² = 18. To Q it is 5² + 0² = 25. P is nearer.
Manhattan: walk along the axes. To P that is 3 + 3 = 6 blocks. To Q it is 5 + 0 = 5 blocks. Q is nearer.
The metric decides the neighbour. Unless a question names another distance, use Euclidean.

scenes.title: Vote at k = 1, 3, 5: the winner can change

steps.caption: Query at (0, 0). The table lists the six training points sorted by squared distance: 2, 4, 5, 9, 9, 32.
k = 1: the nearest point is (1, 1), class A. Votes A 1, B 0. Predict A.
k = 3: the nearest three are A, A, B. Votes A 2, B 1. Predict A.
k = 5: the nearest five are A, A, B, B, B. Votes A 2, B 3. Predict B. The two B's at distance 9 tip the vote.
The label first becomes B at k = 5, so the minimum odd k is 5. Stopping at k = 1 or 3 would have given the wrong answer.

scenes.title: Small k copies the noise, large k smooths it away

objects.text:
small k: follows the noise
large k: smooths to the majority

steps.caption: Nine training points at x = 0 to 8. The B at x = 3 is noise inside a run of A's. We predict each position again with different k.
k = 1: each point's nearest neighbour is itself, so the row copies the data, noise included. 0 wrong.
k = 3: at x = 3 the three nearest are A, B, A, so A wins. The noisy B is outvoted. 1 position differs from the data.
k = 9: all nine points vote, A 5 against B 4, so every position becomes A. The four real B's are overruled. 4 wrong.
Small k is flexible: low bias, high variance. Large k is smooth: high bias, low variance. k = n is a constant.

scenes.title: k-NN regression: average the neighbours' targets

steps.caption: Five training points (x, y). We want the 3-NN prediction at x = 5, the dashed vertical line.
Distances use the inputs only: |x − 5| is 4, 3, 1, 1, 4 for x = 1, 2, 4, 6, 9.
The three smallest distances (1, 1, 3) belong to x = 4, 6 and 2. Their targets are y = 6, 10 and 5.
Average the targets, not the inputs: (6 + 10 + 5) / 3 = 21 / 3 = 7.
The prediction at x = 5 is y = 7.
Six points on a line with labels A, A, A, B, B, A at x = 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8. We use 1-NN and compare two ways of scoring it.
Training error: each point's nearest neighbour is itself, at distance 0. All six are right. Training error = 0 / 6 = 0.
Leave-one-out for x = 0, 1, 2: the nearest other points are all A. Right, right, right.
Leave-one-out for x = 5 and 6: each is the other's nearest neighbour, at distance 1. Both B. Right, right.
Leave-one-out for x = 8 (A): the nearest other point is x = 6, label B, at distance 2. Predict B. Wrong.
Leave-one-out error = 1 / 6 ≈ 0.167. The training error 0 was flattering.
Query q: age 25, income Rs 40,000. Person A: 55 years, Rs 40,500. Person B: 26 years, Rs 46,000. B is clearly the more similar person.
Raw Euclidean distances. A: gaps 30 and 500, so √(900 + 250,000) ≈ 500.9. B: gaps 1 and 6,000, so √(1 + 36,000,000) ≈ 6,000. A looks nearer.
Why: the income gap squared (250,000 for A, 36,000,000 for B) dwarfs the age gap squared (900 or 1). Age is ignored.
Standardise with z = (x − mean) / sd (age: mean 40, sd 10; income: mean 50,000, sd 20,000). Now A is 3.0 away and B only 0.32 away.
Scaling flipped the neighbour: B is the similar person. Always scale before using distances, with the training set's numbers.

steps.caption: One useful feature, no noise (m = 0). Near point A is at distance 1 and far point B at distance 3. B is 3 times farther.

A query arrives at (2, 3). Now the work starts: a squared distance to every point. P1: 1+4 = 5. P2: 4+0 = 4. P3: 0+16 = 16. P4: 9+4 = 13. P5: 1+1 = 2.

objects.text: d² to μ1 = 5,   d² to μ2 = 10:   class 1

steps.caption: Two classes. Class 1 (orange): (1, 1) and (3, 1). Class 2 (pink): (5, 3) and (7, 5).
Query x = (3, 3). Squared distance to μ1: 1² + 2² = 5. To μ2: 3² + 1² = 10. Nearer to μ1, so class 1.
The boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from μ1 to μ2. It passes through the midpoint (4, 2.5) at right angles.
In formula form the squares cancel: f(x) = 8 x1 + 6 x2 − 47. It is linear. f(3, 3) = 24 + 18 − 47 = −5, which is negative, so class 1.
